source_text: adhuc, inquit, secundum hominem dico: dum essemus paruuli, sub elementis mundi eramus positi ad deseruiendum eis. atquin non est hoc humanitus dictum, non enim exemplum est, sed ueritas. quis enim paruulus — utique sensu, quod sunt nationes — non elementis subiectus est mundi, quae pro deo suspicit? illud autem fuit, quod tum secundum hominem dixit: sed tamen testamentum hominis nemo spernit aut superordinat. exemplo enim humani testamenti permanentis diuinum tuebatur: Abrahae dictae sunt promissiones et semini eius. non dixit \'seminibus*, quasi pluribus, sed \'semini\' tamquam uni, quod est Christus. erubescat spongia Marcionis! nisi quod ex abundanti retracto quae abstulit, cum ualidius sit illum ex his reuinci, quae seruauit. cum autem euenit impleri tempus, misit deus filium suum, utique is, qui etiam ipsorum temporum deus est, quibus saeculum constat, qui signa quoque temporum ordinauit, soles et lunas et sidera et stellas, qui filii denique sui reuelationem in extremitatem temporum et disposuit et praedicauit: in nouissimis diebus erit manifestus mons domini, et: in nouissimis diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem, secundum Iohelem. ipsius erat sustinuisse tempus impleri, cuius erat etiam finis temporis sicut initium. ceterum deus ille otiosus nec operationis nec praedicationis ullius atque ita nec temporis alicuius, quid omnino egit, quod efficeret tempus impleri et iam implendum sustineri? si nihil, satis uanum est, ut creatoris tempora sustinuerit seruiens creatori. cui autem rei misit filium suum? ut eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret - hoc est ut efficeret tortuosa in uiam rectam et aspera in uias leues secundum Esaiam, ut uetera transirent et noua orirentur: lex noua ex Sion et sermo domini ex Hierusalem — et ut adoptionem filiorum acciperemus, utique nationes, quae filii non eramus. et ipse enim erit lux nationum et in nomine eius nationes sperabunt. itaque ut certum esset nos filios dei esse, misit spiritum suum in corda nostra clamantem: abba, pater. in nouissimis enim, inquit, diebus effundam de meo spiritu in omnem carnem. cuius gratia, nisi cuius et promissio gratiae?
pass_a_gloss: He says, 'I am still speaking as a human: when we were children, we were under the elements of the world, serving them. But this is not said in a human way, for it is not an example, but truth. For who, being a child - and by this I mean the nations - is not subject to the elements of the world, which they regard as God? However, what he said then as a human was that no one despises or disobeys a human testament. For by the example of a human testament, he was defending the divine one: the promises were made to Abraham and his seed. He did not say 'seeds', as if there were many, but 'seed', as if there were one, which is Christ. Let Marcion's sponge be ashamed! Unless I am retracting what I previously took away, since it is more valid to convict him of what he has preserved. When the time had come, God sent his Son, who is also the God of those times that make up the age, who ordered the signs of the times, the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, and who finally disposed and predicted the revelation of his Son at the end of time: 'In the last days, the mountain of the Lord will be revealed', and 'In the last days, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh', according to Joel. It was his to sustain the time until it was fulfilled, whose end of time was also its beginning. But what did that idle God do, who had no operation, no preaching, and thus no time, to bring about the fulfillment of time and sustain it until it was fulfilled? If he did nothing, it is quite vain that he, as a servant of the Creator, sustained the times of the Creator. To what end did he send his Son? So that he might redeem those who were under the law - that is, so that he might make the crooked straight and the rough smooth, according to Isaiah, so that the old things might pass away and new things might arise: a new law from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem - and so that we might receive the adoption of sons, we who were not sons, namely the nations. And he himself will be the light of the nations, and the nations will hope in his name. Therefore, so that it might be certain that we are sons of God, he sent his Spirit into our hearts, crying 'Abba, Father'. For in the last days, he says, 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh'. To whose grace, if not to the one whose promise is also of grace?

pass_b_english: I still speak in human terms: when we were children, we were placed under the elemental forces of the world to serve them. Yet this is not a merely human saying, for it is not an illustration but the truth. What nation, in its childish understanding, is not subject to the world's elements, which it worships as gods? Still, the point I made in human terms stands: no one sets aside or overrides a human will. By appealing to the binding force of a human will, he safeguards the divine one: the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Scripture does not say 'seeds', implying many, but 'seed', referring to one, who is Christ (Gal 3:16). Let Marcion's sponge blush with shame! Unless, that is, I am now taking back what I previously conceded, since it is more damning to convict him from what he has kept. When the appointed time arrived, God sent his Son — the very one who is God of those ages that constitute the world, who set the celestial signs, the sun and moon, the stars and constellations, and who both arranged and foretold the revelation of his Son at the end of the ages: 'In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be revealed' (Isa 2:2), and 'In the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' (Joel 2:28). It belonged to him to sustain the era until its fulfillment, since the end of time was as much his as the beginning. But what did that idle God accomplish — a God with no action, no proclamation, and therefore no time of his own — to bring about the fullness of time and uphold it until it was due? If he did nothing, it is utterly vain that he, serving the Creator, should have sustained the Creator's times. To what purpose, then, did he send his Son? To redeem those under the law — that is, to make the crooked straight and the rough places smooth (Isa 40:3-5), so that the old order might pass and the new arise: a new law from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa 2:3) — and so that we might receive adoption as sons, we nations who were not sons. For he himself will be the light of the nations, and in his name the nations will hope (Isa 42:6; 49:6). Therefore, to make it certain that we are God's children, he sent his Spirit into our hearts crying, 'Abba, Father' (Rom 8:15). 'For in the last days,' he says, 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh' (Joel 2:28). Whose grace is this, if not his whose promise is also grace?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a more fluent version with appropriate scripture citations (Gal 3:16, Isa 2:2, Joel 2:28, Isa 40:3-5, Isa 2:3, Isa 42:6, 49:6, Rom 8:15) which correspond to the quoted or alluded content in the Latin. All clauses, including the complex rhetorical questions and the distinction between 'seed' and 'seeds', are preserved.
